full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN for the rule system and the clumping. Milling is not a documented feature of this model.**

**1. Model family.** This is the Vicsek model, a minimal flocking model from active matter and statistical physics. Each agent takes the average heading of its neighbours within radius 1, adds angular noise, and moves at constant speed. The setup is a periodic box of side 20 with N=400, so density is 1. Noise is 0.1 rad, which is low. Speed is 0.3 per step, which is fast compared with the usual v0≈0.03. The 800-agent variant is the same model at density 2.

**2. The behaviour.**
- **Rule system.** Vicsek et al. describe particles driven at constant absolute velocity. At each time step they take the average direction of motion of their neighbours, with a random perturbation added. That is this rule system.
- **Clumping.** Clumping at low noise is the standard result for this model. Grégoire & Chaté (2004) found that the transition to collective motion in two dimensions is always discontinuous, including for the minimal Vicsek model. The Chaté et al. (2008) comprehensive study of Vicsek-style models in 2D and 3D found that the onset of collective motion is discontinuous (first-order-like). Their abstract also notes that far from the transition the ordered phase is statistically homogeneous, with anomalously strong density fluctuations. The dense travelling structures (bands and clusters) that cause the clumping are found nearer the transition. A nearest-neighbour ratio of 0.2 fits this clustering.
- **Polar order.** The setup should give strong polar order, or locally ordered clusters. The reported "a_polar = −2.0" looks odd. I assume it is a score relative to some baseline, so it may just mean order below that baseline. Several separate clusters or bands heading in different directions would produce this. I can't tell from the description. Check how the metric is defined.
- **Milling.** This is the one feature that does not fit. Costanzo & Hemelrijk (2018) say milling has been reproduced in more complex models, but not in simpler models based only on alignment, such as the Vicsek model. They obtained it only after minimal modifications. Milling occurs when both the field of view and the maximal angular velocity are decreased. The 2025 review "Topological defects in polar active matter" agrees. Rotational motion is not manifested spontaneously and instead appears through alignment with confining boundaries.

A high milling score in a periodic Vicsek box is therefore most likely a measurement artefact. A rotation or angular-momentum measure about a centre will read high when there are several moving clusters. It could also be a transient swirl. I did not find a source reporting stable milling in plain Vicsek dynamics. I did not search specifically for transient vortices in this model, so I cannot rule them out. Related work on "swirling structures" exists for the Vicsek model with delay, which is a different system.

**Citations checked against search results.**
- Vicsek, Czirók, Ben-Jacob, Cohen, Shochet (1995), PRL 75, 1226. Original model.
- Grégoire & Chaté (2004), PRL 92, 025702. Discontinuous onset.
- Chaté, Ginelli, Grégoire, Raynaud (2008), PRE 77, 046113. Comprehensive study of the ordered phase.
- Vicsek & Zafeiris (2012), Physics Reports 517, 71–140. Review. I verified the bibliographic details but not its content on bands or milling.
- Costanzo & Hemelrijk (2018), J. Phys. D. Milling needs extra ingredients.

**Confidence: medium-high.** The identification of the model and the clumping is solid. The medium part is the milling and the negative polar score. I can't see the metric definitions, so I can't say whether milling is an artefact or a real transient.
